en: That pitch-black haze—
What seemed haze was people.
See the dug pit!
Bellowing their battle cry,
See the Chinese host sweeping on.
See the haze, see the embers!
See the bullets striking unerringly!
See the reeds, see the flood!
See the Chinese people sweeping on.
See the foot-soldiers no horse could carry!
Within that host,
Never leaving a grappling foe alone,
Some six thousand heroes came out.
Insatiable to the last,
A people called swift foot-runners had come.
When the swift foot-runners swept forward,
The earth broke and shook.
With one eye in the forehead,
Many strange peoples had come.
The Chinese shouted and rumbled.
Unable to stand and look back,
The faith of Islam, small as a palm,
The poor bastards despaired of life.
The Chinese people pressed upon them,
Coming with a clamor.
“We shall never see home!” they said;
Among the palm-sized Muslim band,
Some stood sobbing bitterly.
The mighty men with courage
Spread out along the edges;
The fierce ones never sated with blood,
Venom pouring from their mouths.
The weaklings without courage,
A black day fallen on their heads,
Had their hearts sorely troubled.
Those men who worried like Asan the Sorrowful,
“I had only one horse!” they said;
More than these were languishing.
All the lion-like heroes said,
“We have had our pleasure exchanging shots;
If death comes, we die!”
More than these were rejoicing.
The rash and senseless,
More than these were panicking.
The weaklings without courage,
Penned in the middle,
More than these were fleeing.
Their steeds would not stand still;
More than these were rearing and plunging.
The heroes who had courage,
Without fearing death,
Still more were rejoicing.
At the sight of the enemy,
They grew wild and strained forward,
Thrashing like a woman whose husband had died;
Six men to hold one person—
There were many more like that.
With no sense entering their breasts,
Still more were losing heart.
Bent over their spears,
Those making ready were beyond counting.
With eyes blazing like wolves’,
Biting through their tongues,
There were still more champions.
Divided into group upon group,
If you sat and watched their forms,
The varied people of imperial China
Looked as though they would suck you dry.
Riding red-roan horses,
Their long tails tied in tight knots,
Their fiercest men formed separate ranks;
Swaying across the hills,
They too had surged in.
In black robes and broad shirts,
The governors’ army gathered,
And surged upon them all together.
Bearing iron ropes and nets,
Biting through their lips,
Their eyes seething deep within,
Never releasing those they grappled with,
Never sated with human flesh,
Ajgu and Jajojo
Had surged in together.
The Chinese people came with their armies,
Overwhelming to anyone who measured them.
If you looked closely, your Muslims
Could be bound captive by that approaching host.
When you looked at the Chinese,
The earth seemed to turn and split apart.
In that coming battle,
The handful of Muslims
Scattered like frightened sheep.
When the mighty Chinese army,
That formidable host, surged in without measure,
Their bitter brine of misery was about to boil.
Through the red and mottled haze,
Arrows from bows streamed down.
“My banner on a crimson spear,
Dear Alake, keep me safe!” they said,
And sought shelter with your Alake.
Girded in golden iron,
Girded with a belt of gold,
Azizkhan’s Almambet,
Light shining on his moonlike face,
Blood suffusing his dark eyes,
Light shining on his bloody face,
His complexion like oiled wheat,
His eyes like twilight mist,
Without looking round him,
When the Chinese surged upon him,
Your valiant falcon
Did not spare his life at all.
“Against the darkening black unbelievers
I have now waged holy war,” he said.
“If God so wills, here and now
I have offered up my precious life,” he said.
“To Beijing, where the Prophet never trod,
I have ridden on holy war,” he said.
“If God so wills, here and now
I have offered up my one precious life!” he said.
Stake-necked Sarala
The noble lion made rear;
Lean-haunched Sarala
The noble lion sent wheeling.
The black-cheeked battle-axe
Hung at your Alake’s wrist;
The double-edged Zulpuqor
Was drawn ready from its sheath.
The yellow willow he had planted yesterday,
His willow still stood behind;
The throne fashioned of pure gold,
His throne still stood behind.
He scattered what he had gathered,
Seeking faith alone.
A merciless onslaught
Had he not come to unleash?
Karykan’s painted musket,
Taken as a gift from Beijing,
My renowned champion Alma
Had he not brought it with him?
When slung, the painted musket
Was the mirror of his moonlike shoulder;
When he entered battle with the shooting foe,
It was a comfort to his entrusted life.
In play, a matchlock;
In earnest, a breaker of foes.
The painted spear swayed in his hand,
The gold-mouthed painted musket
Gleamed upon his moonlike shoulder.
With brown eyes free of pale flecks,
With a fair face free of freckles,
With no dirt upon his eyelashes,
Khan Aziz’s only son,
Blue flame hissing from his mouth,
His mighty teeth, broad as a door,
Crumbling like millet grains,
“This handful of Muslims—
How can I stand and let them be taken?” he said.
“If I can find a way, the Chinese
I shall slaughter all the way to Beijing,” he said.
“Against six myriad black unbelievers
I shall exchange shots and wage war,” he said.
Your Alake entered the battle.
“Without standing by them as support,
How can I remain alive?” he said.
Khan Baltay’s Chubak—
Did you see his blood stir?
Baabedin’s Baychoro,
Warrior Shuutu, his cap as broad as a yurt covering,
Old Kyrgyl, leader of the forty,
Yraman’s son Yrchy,
Akayar, who lifted camels,
Who drank poison when told to drink water,
Who spilled stomach contents when told to shed blood,
Who took heads when told to take caps,
Who waded through embers when told to wade through bullets,
Who never drew back from a dispute,
Who never turned away from death,
Their horses grown fat and fit,
Each alone the equal of forty,
Who had made Talas their homeland,
Who had raised as khan and made their lion
Manas, the true blue-maned hero,
Who had hunted white deer,
Who had raised an uproar wherever they met—
All forty valiant men were there,
The precious Chubak and Almambet,
All the champions were there.
Koshoi and Toshtuk, their names in accord,
The two matching khans had come.
“If death arrives, I shall die,” he said.
“For this handful of Muslims,
While this precious life remains,
I shall serve as imam,” he said.
Aykojo, who had come from Mecca,
Had come then to lead their prayers.
Warrior Urbu, son of Eybit Khan,
Jamgyrchy of the Eshteks,
When their mighty khan Kongurbay
Made the whole earth wretched,
And the Chinese surged upon them,
All the great khans
Gathered together in anguish.
A mighty torment fell upon them,
And together they despaired of life.
The reason for their despair:
The sky was clear, the earth overcast;
Not a single blade upon the ground was visible,
Earth swirled and dust flew,
Not one soul among the people could be seen.
There were gray-mottled pennants and standards,
An uproar of cries of “Alas! Alas!”
White-mottled pennants and black standards,
Shouts and a tumultuous roar.
This was the Great Campaign itself,
The hour when unbelievers and Muslims
Were to meet face to face.
The bloodied men were drenched in blood,
And the heroes did not draw back;
They stood and fought without fleeing.
All the heroes grew weary,
Those very heroes,
With painted spears of black iron,
The heroes stood without fleeing
And drove them straight into each other’s hearts.
The earth’s surface rumbled,
All the people were scattered apart.
Then, golden-crested, with a belt like embers,
Azizkhan’s only son,
Ninety governors against him alone,
My Alake held them off.
When he leaned right and thrust,
He brought down more than ten;
When he leaned left and thrust,
He laid their sultans low.
Within that very campaign,
Lean-haunched Sarala
Your Alake kept saddled.
The incantation called Uyba,
Throwing them into turmoil,
Your Alake went on reciting.
Into their center Almambet
Carved his way;
Around their edges the forty companions
Slaughtered their way forward.
Into their very midst the seven khans
Plundered their way;
Against one flank Chubak
Battered his way forward.
On the side by the steep bank, Ajybai
Came hemming them in;
Against one flank old Kyrgyl
Slaughtered his way forward.
The whole plain became dust,
All the level ground became blood.
